newsitem.title: USA: USDA increasingly concerned about EU subsidies.
newsitem.headline: USDA increasingly concerned about EU subsidies.

text.p: A recent sharp increase in European grain subsidy levels has heightened concern among top officials at the Agriculture Department about the European Union's use of export subsidies, the department's senior trade advisor said Wednesday.

"It would be fair to say the increase in the European subsidies caught our attention," said Paul Drazek, trade advisor to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. "We're very concerned about European subsidies not only on wheat, but on other products."

The EU last week unexpectedly hiked its wheat subsidy levels to $16 per tonne, a move that Drazek said prompted trans-Atlantic phone conversations between him and senior EU officials. Drazek said he reiterated the U.S. concern about subsidies and Washington's position that subsidies are not necessary.

Agriculture Secretary Glickman is going to meet with EU Agriculture Commission Franz Fischler next month in Rome while attending the World Food Summit, and Drazek said export subsidies will be high on their agenda.

But in response to calls from the National Association of Wheat Growers on Tuesday that USDA officially reactivate its Export Enhancement Program, and begin to aggressively fight EU subsidies, Drazek said the issue is not that simple.

"The decision to pursue an EEP initiative is a very serious matter, and any decision would have to be taken after very, very careful examiniaton of all the factors involved," he told Reuters. "One of them clearly is what the Europeans are doing -- this is not the only factor, but it's an important one."

Drazek said that the tight supply situation of wheat in the United States and effects of subsidies on the domestic U.S. market are key factors to consider in making any decision on whether or not to restart export subsidies.
Many grain industry analysts have been skeptical of the benefits of reactivating export subsidies at this point.

They claim that the short U.S. supplies and surplus foreign stocks would limit how aggressively Washington would be able to push subsidies, and could in fact tighten U.S. supplies even more and ultimately encourage more grain imports into the United States.

A study by the agricultural consulting group Sparks Companies said the use of EEP this crop year would be of little benefit to exports, would drive world wheat prices lower, establish a two-tier pricing structure that could spark Canadian wheat shipments into the U.S., and potentially decrease corn exports if wheat prices were cheap enough.

"There are a lot of pitfalls with using the EEP at this point," said a grain industry official. "There are so many fish-hooks in this current market environment, I'm not even sure if it's prudent to act."
The National Association of Wheat Growers sent a letter to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman on Tuesday, urging the department to officially restart the EEP.

"The administration's wait-and-see policy is not strong enough," said NAWG executive vice president Carl Schwenson. "Our view is that the administration should escalate its threat againnst the European Union, and do so by putting the machinery in place necessary to get EEP up and running again."
